questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Data splits
questions.question: A streaming service's model owner reports that its churn model catches 96% of leaving customers, but many test records belong to customers also in the training data. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The model documentation does not record how the split was made
options.B: The test set may be too small for a reliable estimate
options.C: Reported results may overstate performance on unseen customers
options.D: The catch rate was not compared with a vendor benchmark

questions.key_concept: Training, validation and test data must be kept separate; leakage between them inflates reported performance.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the test data was truly unseen by the model before trusting any score reported from it.
questions.correct_explanation: When the same customers appear in training and test data, the model is partly graded on cases it has already learned, so the 96% catch rate can overstate how it will perform on customers it has not seen. Management would be relying on unreliable evidence. An undocumented split method would be a real gap, but documenting a leaky split would not make its score any more trustworthy.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the split method should be documented. But documenting a leaky split does not fix it; the greater concern is that the catch rate itself is unreliable.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because small test sets give shaky estimates. But the problem here is overlap with training data, which inflates scores however large the test set is.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because benchmarks seem objective. But a vendor benchmark measures other data and models; it cannot show whether this model's own test was clean.

tips: Eliminate: B blames test-set size, but overlap inflates scores at any size, and D leans on a vendor benchmark, which says nothing about this model's own test design.
Final two: C beats A because the overlap makes the headline catch rate unreliable evidence; documenting the split would record the flaw, not remove it.
Exam cue: when test data shares records or people with training data, treat the reported performance as unproven until it is retested on truly unseen data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.1 (Test sets, metrics and TEVV tools documented)

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Third-party data
questions.question: A shipping firm plans to retrain its delay-prediction model with a purchased dataset, but the broker cannot say where the records came from. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the data owner obtain provenance and licensing evidence before use
options.B: Have the data team profile the dataset for quality and representativeness
options.C: Rely on the broker's contract warranty that the data is accurate
options.D: Buy a second dataset so errors in either one are diluted

questions.key_concept: Third-party AI training data needs documented provenance and rights to use before it enters the pipeline.
questions.pre_read: Notice whether the data's origin is known before judging how good the data looks.
questions.correct_explanation: Without provenance, the firm cannot show it may lawfully use the data, that the records are untampered, or trace a later fault back to its source. Origin and licensing evidence is therefore the first gate. Profiling for quality and representativeness is needed too, but it describes what the data looks like, not where it came from or whether it may be used, so it comes second.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because data quality checks are essential. But profiling cannot reveal the data's origin, licensing or tampering, so it should follow provenance evidence, not replace it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because contracts shift some liability. But an accuracy warranty is a vendor claim; it gives no lineage and does not cover rights to use or tampering.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because larger datasets can average out noise. But adding more data of unknown origin multiplies the provenance problem instead of solving it.

tips: Eliminate: C treats a vendor warranty as assurance, though vendor claims are only inputs, and D adds volume, which cannot fix data whose origin is unknown.
Final two: A beats B because origin and rights to use are the first gate; quality profiling describes the data but cannot prove where it came from.
Exam cue: for third-party training data, ask for provenance and rights before quality tests; unknown lineage blocks use however clean the data looks.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 4.1 (Legal and technology risks of components including third-party data mapped); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SR-4 (Provenance)

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Data fitness
questions.question: A telecom's call-center speech-to-text model was trained on recordings from one regional office and will now serve customers in five countries. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Add more recordings from the same speakers to enlarge the dataset
options.B: Rely on the vendor's published accuracy for the base speech model
options.C: Measure overall transcription accuracy on a fresh sample of calls
options.D: Compare the accent mix in training data with actual callers

questions.key_concept: Training data must represent the population a model will serve; volume does not fix a skewed mix.
questions.pre_read: Compare who is in the training data with who the model will actually serve.
questions.correct_explanation: Recordings from one regional office probably carry a narrow mix of accents, and a model learns the patterns in its training data, so callers who speak differently may get far more errors. Comparing the training data's accent mix with the callers it will serve shows the gap before launch. An overall accuracy figure on fresh calls is useful, but a single average can hide poor results for smaller groups.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more data often helps. But more recordings of the same speakers repeat the same accent gap; representativeness, not volume, is the issue.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor tested the base model. But published accuracy reflects the vendor's test data, not this firm's customers, so it is an input, not assurance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fresh data avoids leakage. But one overall figure can look strong while customers with underrepresented accents get far worse results.

tips: Eliminate: A adds volume without changing the accent mix, and B relies on vendor accuracy measured on someone else's data.
Final two: D beats C because comparing the training data with the actual callers exposes the gap directly; an overall average can hide poor results for smaller groups.
Exam cue: when a model will serve people unlike those in its training data, check representativeness first; volume and averages do not reveal who is left out.

questions.question: A retailer's machine learning operations (MLOps) pipeline promotes any retrained model to production once its code passes unit and integration tests. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Unit tests may not cover every branch of the pipeline code
options.B: Releases are not gated on data quality and model performance results
options.C: Frequent automated releases leave no time for model documentation
options.D: The pipeline relies on open-source tools instead of a licensed platform

questions.key_concept: AI releases need stage gates on data and model performance, not only code tests.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the release test actually examines: the code, the data or the model's behavior.
questions.correct_explanation: A retrained model can behave differently while its code stays identical, because its behavior comes from the data it learned. Code tests cannot show whether the new version is accurate, fair or trained on sound data, so the release needs a gate on data and performance evidence. Incomplete unit-test coverage is a real code-quality gap, but even full coverage would leave the model's behavior untested.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because coverage matters for software. But the deciding risk is untested model behavior; perfect code coverage still says nothing about accuracy or data quality.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fast releases can squeeze paperwork. But automated pipelines can record documentation as they run; release frequency itself is not the control gap here.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tool maturity varies. But open-source tooling can be well controlled; the weakness is what the gate checks, not who supplies the tools.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes fast pipelines cannot document, though they can record artifacts automatically, and D blames the tooling source, which is not a control weakness in itself.
Final two: B beats A because a model's behavior comes from data, so code tests, however complete, cannot show the new version performs acceptably.
Exam cue: when a model is released like ordinary code, look for the missing data and performance gate before production.

questions.question: A customs broker plans to license a vendor's pre-trained model to classify import declarations; the vendor offers an accuracy summary but no model card or training-data description. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Accept the vendor's accuracy summary as the validation evidence
options.B: Run a pilot comparing the model with staff decisions before signing
options.C: Require documented training data, intended use and limits before signing
options.D: Retrain the model on the broker's own training data to cut dependence

questions.key_concept: Model documentation, such as a model card, is a precondition for assessing a third-party model.
questions.pre_read: Notice the timing: what can the organization still require before it signs?
questions.correct_explanation: Before the contract is signed, the broker has leverage to require the documentation that makes the model auditable: what data trained it, what it was built for and where it fails. Without that, no later test can be scoped against the intended use. A pilot against staff decisions is valuable evidence, but it comes after the documentation; if the vendor still withholds it, testing on the broker's own data becomes the main evidence.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the summary looks like test evidence. But vendor accuracy figures are claims about the vendor's own data; they are inputs, not assurance for this use.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because real-world comparison is strong evidence. But a pilot cannot show what data trained the model or its known limits, and those terms must be secured first.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because owning the training seems safer. But retraining is a technical fix before governance, and the broker still lacks evidence of what the base model learned.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a vendor's accuracy figure as assurance, though it is only an input, and D jumps to a technical fix before the model is even understood.
Final two: C beats B because documentation of data, purpose and limits must be secured first; a pilot shows results but cannot reveal how the model was built.
Exam cue: for bought or pre-trained models, make model documentation a condition of the deal; vendor scores and pilots come after.

questions.question: A benefits agency retiring its eligibility-scoring model will keep the source code and decision logs for seven years but delete the trained model files. What is the IS auditor's BEST-supported conclusion about open appeals?

options.A: Past scores can be shown but not reproduced or independently explained
options.B: Code and logs together allow any past score to be regenerated
options.C: Logged outcomes are enough to answer appeals without the model
options.D: The replacement model can rescore old cases to answer appeals

questions.key_concept: Code and decision logs cannot reproduce past AI decisions; keep the exact trained model version while decisions can be challenged.
questions.pre_read: List what each retained record can show about a past decision, and what it cannot.
questions.correct_explanation: Decision logs record what the model decided and the code records how it was built, but the scores came from the trained model's learned parameters. Without the model files, no one can rerun an input to reproduce a score or explain it for an appeal. Code plus logs, option B, is the runner-up: it sounds complete, but retraining from the code, even on the same data, may not reproduce the model.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because code and inputs seem enough to rerun anything. But a model's behavior comes from training; rebuilt from code, it may be a different model.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because logs show each outcome. But appeals ask why a decision was made, which needs the model that made it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the replacement is validated and available. But it is a different model; its scores do not show how the old model decided.

tips: Eliminate: C falls because appeals need the reason for a decision, not just its outcome, and D rescores with a different model that never made the original decisions.
Final two: A beats B because a model's behavior lives in its trained files; retraining from code, even on the same data, may not reproduce it.
Exam cue: logs show what an AI decided and code shows how it was built; reproducing or explaining a decision needs the exact trained model version.

questions.question: A pet-supplies retailer logs edits to its care-advice assistant's system prompt as pre-approved standard changes, like website text updates. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the standard-change route and log each editor's name
options.B: Treat prompt edits as changes needing testing and approval
options.C: Rely on the model provider's filter to block harmful answers
options.D: Freeze the current prompt and refuse any further edits

questions.key_concept: Prompt edits change AI behavior broadly and unpredictably, so they fail the test for pre-approved standard changes and need testing and approval.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the outcome of an edit can be known in advance, as a standard change requires.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard changes suit low-risk edits whose outcome is known in advance, such as website text. A system prompt is different: one line can shift every answer the assistant gives, in ways nobody can predict from the wording, so each edit needs testing against expected behavior and the model owner's approval. Logging editors under the standard route adds accountability but still lets an untested edit reach pet owners.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because standard changes with logging suit routine edits. But a prompt edit's effect is not known in advance, so it fails the standard-change test.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because filters catch some harmful output. But a filter blocks certain content; it cannot show that an edited prompt kept advice accurate and on-policy.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because no edits means no risk from edits. But business needs change, and banning updates pushes edits outside control rather than managing them.

tips: Eliminate: C leans on output filtering, which blocks some content but does not test changed behavior, and D bans change instead of controlling it.
Final two: B beats A because a standard change needs a known, low-risk outcome; a prompt edit can shift every answer, so it needs testing and approval first.
Exam cue: anything that changes how an AI system behaves, such as prompts, thresholds, retraining or settings, is a change and rarely a pre-approved standard one.

questions.question: An online marketplace flags prohibited listings with a vendor-hosted large language model; flag rates fell sharply after the vendor upgraded the model without notice. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the vendor's statement that the upgrade improved accuracy
options.B: Retune the flagging threshold until rates match last month
options.C: Monitor flag rates daily so that future vendor changes are detected sooner
options.D: Require version pinning and owner testing before vendor upgrades apply

questions.key_concept: Vendor model updates are changes to the organization's system and need version control and testing before use.
questions.pre_read: Notice who changed the model and whether the organization had any chance to test it first.
questions.correct_explanation: A silent vendor upgrade is an uncontrolled change to the marketplace's own control. The best response brings vendor updates into change management: contract terms for pinned versions or advance notice, and testing by the model owner before an upgrade goes live. Daily monitoring is worth adding, but it only detects the next silent change after the change has already altered results.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor knows its model. But the vendor's claim is an input; falling flag rates are evidence that the upgrade changed the control's results.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it restores the old rate quickly. But retuning is itself an unapproved change aimed at a number, and last month's rate may not be the right one.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because monitoring catches shifts. But it is detective: it finds the next silent change only after it has altered results, and the vendor can still change the model freely.

tips: Eliminate: A takes a vendor claim as assurance against contrary evidence, and B makes an unapproved threshold change to hit a number.
Final two: D beats C because preventive control over vendor upgrades stops the next silent change; monitoring only notices it after it has altered results.
Exam cue: a vendor's model update is a change to your system; expect contract terms, version control and owner testing, not just monitoring.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Versions and baselines
questions.question: A grocery chain retrains its demand-forecast model nightly; after a costly bad forecast, the team cannot reproduce the deployed version or say what it learned from. What should the IS auditor recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Retrain weekly instead of nightly so fewer versions need tracking
options.B: Keep the previous model version and its settings ready to restore quickly
options.C: Register each model artifact with its data snapshot, code and settings
options.D: Use the source code repository history as the version record

questions.key_concept: Configuration management for AI records each model version with its data, code and settings so it can be traced, rebuilt and rolled back.
questions.pre_read: Ask what you would need to rebuild exactly the model that made a given output.
questions.correct_explanation: A model version is the trained model plus the code, training data snapshot, settings and environment that produced it, not code alone. A registry linking each deployed version to all of these lets the team trace a bad forecast to its cause, rebuild or compare versions and know which one to trust. Keeping the previous model for rollback helps recovery, but without lineage nobody can show that the earlier version is sound.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fewer versions seem easier to control. But slowing retraining avoids the problem rather than controlling it, and weekly versions would still lack lineage.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because rollback limits damage. But without lineage the team cannot show the earlier version is any better, or find what broke this one.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because code history is a strong record for software. But a model's behavior also depends on its data snapshot and settings, which the code repository does not capture.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains less often instead of controlling versions, and D treats code history as enough, though a model also depends on data and settings.
Final two: C beats B because a registry with lineage makes every version traceable; a rollback target is only trustworthy when its lineage is known.
Exam cue: for AI configuration management, a version means the trained model plus its code, data and settings; look for a registry that ties them to each release.

questions.question: A university's admissions staff confirm 99.7% of an AI model's rejection recommendations, spending under a minute per file. Which conclusion does this evidence BEST support?

options.A: Human review may be a rubber stamp rather than real oversight
options.B: The model may have drifted since it was last validated
options.C: High agreement confirms that the model makes sound decisions
options.D: The review step adds cost and could safely be removed

questions.key_concept: Human oversight is effective only if reviewers can and do challenge the model; rubber-stamping is automation bias.
questions.pre_read: Look at how the humans behave, not only at how the model performs.
questions.correct_explanation: Near-total agreement at under a minute per file suggests reviewers are accepting the model's output rather than judging each application, the pattern called automation bias. Oversight exists on paper but may not work in practice. Reading the same agreement as proof the model is sound gets the evidence backward: agreement confirms quality only when reviewers judge independently, and these reviewers barely look.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because drift is a common AI risk. But nothing here measures changing data or outcomes, and reviewers who rubber-stamp would not reveal drift anyway.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because agreement looks like validation. But agreement from reviewers who barely look at files is not independent evidence that the decisions are sound.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the step seems to add little. But rejections affect applicants' futures, so a person able to understand, override and stop the model must remain.

tips: Eliminate: B suggests drift, though nothing here measures changing data or outcomes, and D removes oversight from a decision that seriously affects applicants.
Final two: A beats C because agreement is evidence only when reviewers judge independently; fast, near-total agreement shows deference, not proof the model is sound.
Exam cue: very high agreement plus very little review time signals automation bias; oversight must be effective, not just present.

questions.question: A water utility rechecks its leak-prediction model monthly on the launch test set, and accuracy has held at 92% for 18 months. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain the leak-prediction model monthly regardless of results
options.B: Track drift and accuracy on recent production outcomes
options.C: Have an independent team revalidate the model on the launch test set
options.D: Report the stable accuracy to the board as evidence of no drift

questions.key_concept: Drift shows in recent production data and outcomes; a frozen launch test set cannot reveal it.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the reported accuracy could change at all if the conditions the model serves changed.
questions.correct_explanation: A launch test set reflects conditions at launch, so a model scored on it monthly keeps reporting the same accuracy however pipes, weather or sensors change. Drift shows only in recent production data and outcomes, tracked against tolerances. Independent revalidation, option C, is the runner-up: independence adds credibility, but on the same frozen data it repeats the same blind spot.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retraining refreshes the model. But retraining on a schedule is an uncontrolled change and still gives no measure of whether predictions hold.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because independent validation is strong evidence. But validators using the launch test set still measure old conditions and cannot see drift.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the figure is stable and documented. But stability on old data says nothing about current predictions and can hide drift.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains on a schedule without any quality measure, and D treats stable scores on old data as proof there is no drift.
Final two: B beats C because drift appears only in recent production outcomes; independent validators using the launch test set share the blind spot.
Exam cue: when accuracy is measured only on the original test set, recommend monitoring recent production outcomes against tolerances.

questions.question: A payment app's AI model automatically freezes accounts it flags as fraudulent, and affected customers can reach only a chatbot that restates the decision. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Raise the model's flagging threshold to reduce wrongful freezes
options.B: Have the vendor certify the model's false-positive rate annually
options.C: Publish a plain-language notice explaining how the model works
options.D: Provide an appeal to staff with authority to reverse freezes

questions.key_concept: People affected by high-impact automated decisions need an appeal route to a human who can override.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a wrongly affected customer can actually do to get the outcome changed.
questions.correct_explanation: Freezing an account harms a customer directly, so people affected by an automated decision need a route to a person who can review and reverse it. That appeal route also feeds errors back into monitoring. A plain-language notice improves transparency, but explaining how the model works gives a wrongly frozen customer no remedy, so the harm continues until someone with authority acts.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fewer flags mean fewer wrongful freezes. But a threshold change needs its own approval, and wrongly flagged customers would still have no way to object.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because certification sounds independent. But a vendor's figure is an input, not assurance, and it does nothing for a customer whose account is frozen today.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because transparency matters to affected people. But understanding the model does not unfreeze an account; without review by a person, the harm continues.

tips: Eliminate: A tunes the model without giving affected customers any remedy, and B relies on a vendor figure, which is an input and helps no individual customer.
Final two: D beats C because an appeal to someone with authority can correct a wrong decision; a notice explains the model but changes nothing for the customer.
Exam cue: when AI decisions directly harm people, look for an appeal route to a human with authority to override.

questions.question: A ride-hailing company's driver-deactivation model shows 94% overall precision in validation, yet most wrongful-deactivation complaints come from one demographic group of drivers. Which additional test result should the IS auditor request FIRST?

options.A: Error rates broken out by driver age, gender and region
options.B: Precision on a recent out-of-time sample of deactivations
options.C: Overall accuracy recalculated on the model's training data
options.D: Benchmark results for the same algorithm on a public dataset

questions.key_concept: Fairness testing compares error rates across groups; a single overall metric can hide unequal harm.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose errors an overall figure might be hiding.
questions.correct_explanation: Deactivation removes drivers' income, and complaints concentrated in one group suggest errors do not fall evenly. A strong overall figure can hide much worse error rates for some ages, genders or regions, which only a breakdown by group reveals. An out-of-time sample checks whether performance holds on newer data, which matters too, but it still reports one overall number and could hide the same group gaps.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because recent data guards against drift and leakage. But it still yields one overall figure, which can hide poor results for particular groups of drivers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is easy to produce. But scores on training data measure memory, not performance, and overstate how the model treats new cases.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because public benchmarks are independent. But they measure the algorithm on other data, not this model's effect on this company's drivers.

tips: Eliminate: C scores the model on data it learned from, which inflates results, and D measures the algorithm on someone else's data, not this company's drivers.
Final two: A beats B because only a group-level breakdown shows whether some drivers bear more errors; an out-of-time sample still gives a single average.
Exam cue: when an AI decision affects people, ask for results broken out by group; one overall metric can hide unfair outcomes.

questions.question: A savings cooperative's data scientists built a member-risk model and present their automated machine learning platform's built-in validation report as independent evidence. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST before deployment?

options.A: Have the IS auditor validate and approve the model for release
options.B: Have the team rerun the platform's validation on an out-of-time sample
options.C: Have validators independent of the builders challenge and retest it
options.D: Accept the platform's automated report as the independent validation

questions.key_concept: Independent validation needs people separate from the builders; a platform's built-in report runs on the builders' own data, metrics and settings.
questions.pre_read: Ask who chose the data, metrics and pass marks behind the report, and whether they had a stake in the result.
questions.correct_explanation: The platform's report runs on the data, metrics and thresholds the builders configured, so it is self-review in automated form: their assumptions shape both the model and its test. Validators independent of the builders, who challenge the design and data and retest, give management credible evidence. Rerunning the platform on an out-of-time sample is a stronger test, but the same builders still choose what is checked.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because auditors are independent. But validating and approving the model would make the IS auditor part of the control and impair independence; management arranges validation.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because out-of-time testing is sound practice. But the builders still choose the data, metrics and pass marks, so the lack of independence remains.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because system-generated evidence is often more reliable. But the platform tests what the builders configured; automation does not make their choices independent.

tips: Eliminate: A has the IS auditor validating and approving a model, which impairs independence, and D treats tool output as independent, though the builders configured it.
Final two: C beats B because independence from the builders is what makes validation credible; a better test sample still leaves the builders choosing what is checked.
Exam cue: an automated validation report is only as independent as the people who configured it; the IS auditor assesses validation but never performs or approves it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.3 (Independent assessors not on the front-line development team)

questions.question: Reviewing a pre-release test report, the IS auditor finds the model owner chose the approval accuracy threshold after seeing the scores. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The model owner, not the auditor, chose the accuracy threshold
options.B: The pass mark may fit these results, not the business need
options.C: The test data may not reflect conditions in production
options.D: The threshold was set below the vendor's published benchmark

questions.key_concept: AI acceptance criteria must be defined before testing, from business need and risk tolerance.
questions.pre_read: Notice the order of events: when was the bar set, and when were the results known?
questions.correct_explanation: Acceptance criteria must come from the business need and risk tolerance before testing, so results are judged against a fixed bar. A threshold chosen after seeing the scores can be bent to let any result pass, so the approval proves little. Test data that does not match production is a common weakness, but nothing in the report suggests it; the stated fact is the moving goalpost.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because ownership questions are common. But the model owner should set acceptance criteria; the auditor assesses them and never sets them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because deployment-like test conditions matter. But the stem gives no sign of unrepresentative data; the stated weakness is when the bar was set.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because benchmarks look objective. But a vendor's benchmark reflects other data and uses; criteria should come from this system's need and risk tolerance.

tips: Eliminate: A wants the auditor to own acceptance criteria, which is the model owner's job, and D compares against a vendor benchmark instead of the business need.
Final two: B beats C because criteria set after the results can be fitted to pass anything; the stem gives no sign of unrepresentative test data.
Exam cue: in AI testing, acceptance criteria are fixed before testing begins; criteria chosen after results make the test meaningless.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.5 (Organizational risk tolerances determined and documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.13 (Effectiveness of TEVV metrics and processes evaluated)

questions.question: An engineering firm's internal AI assistant reads supplier PDFs from a shared folder and can send emails on staff's behalf. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Outsiders breaching the firewall to reach the model's servers
options.B: Competitors copying the model by querying it many times
options.C: Staff crafting prompts that trick the assistant into sending improper emails
options.D: Hidden instructions in a supplier file steering the assistant's emails

questions.key_concept: Indirect prompt injection plants instructions in content an AI system reads; tool access turns it into real actions.
questions.pre_read: Ask who controls the content the AI reads and what the AI is allowed to do.
questions.correct_explanation: The assistant combines untrusted content, supplier files, with the power to act by sending email. A third party can plant instructions in a document that the assistant may follow, sending data out under a staff member's name: indirect prompt injection. Direct prompting by staff is a real risk too, but staff are known, authorized users, while the outside attacker needs no access at all.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because perimeter attacks are familiar. But prompt injection travels inside ordinary content the assistant is allowed to read; no firewall breach is needed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because model extraction is a real AI threat. But it needs heavy query access, and this internal assistant is not exposed to competitors.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because jailbreaks are well known. But staff are identified, authorized users; the supplier file lets an outsider steer the assistant with no access at all.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a perimeter attack, but injected instructions arrive in content the assistant may read, and B needs outside query access this internal tool lacks.
Final two: D beats C because untrusted supplier files let an outsider steer an assistant that can act; staff prompts come from known, authorized users.
Exam cue: when an AI reads outside content and can take actions, rank indirect prompt injection high.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.4 (Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks and Mitigations); MITRE ATLAS AML.T0051.001 (LLM Prompt Injection: Indirect)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.2 Prompt Injection and Jailbreaks (rank by what the system reads and what it can do). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA pilot, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test, standards audit, concept review).

questions.question: An internet provider's AI agent answers billing questions from customer chats under a service account that can issue refunds; its system prompt forbids refunds. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Remove refund rights from the service account the agent uses
options.B: Keep the prompt rule and review the service account's refunds monthly
options.C: Rely on the vendor's assurance that the agent obeys its prompt
options.D: Place the agent's server behind a stronger network firewall

questions.key_concept: Excessive agency is limited by least-privilege access for the agent's identity and tools, not by instructions.
questions.pre_read: List what the agent's account can do, then ask what happens if the agent is tricked.
questions.correct_explanation: The prompt rule is enforced only by the model, and customer chats are untrusted input that can carry injected instructions, so a manipulated agent could still issue refunds its account allows. Removing refund rights from the account the agent uses, least privilege, makes the limit hold whatever the agent is told. Monthly review of refunds would detect misuse, but only after money has gone.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a preventive rule plus detective review looks layered. But the prompt rule is not access control, and review finds improper refunds only after they are paid.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor knows its product. But vendor assurance is an input; agents can be manipulated, and the organization stays accountable for what the account can do.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because firewalls protect servers. But manipulation arrives through the normal conversations the agent is meant to receive, and the excess rights remain.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on vendor assurance, which is only an input, and D adds network defense, though manipulation arrives through the agent's normal conversations.
Final two: A beats B because removed rights hold even when the agent is manipulated; a prompt rule can be overridden, and monthly review finds refunds already paid.
Exam cue: for AI agents, judge the tools and permissions, not the instructions; a prompt rule is not an access control.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.5 (Security of Agents); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)

questions.question: An agritech firm sells access to its proprietary crop-yield model through an application programming interface (API) with full-precision scores and unlimited queries. Which threat in this design concerns the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Heavy query volume slowing the service for other subscribers
options.B: Subscribers rebuilding a working copy of the model from its answers
options.C: Subscribers poisoning the model through unusual queries
options.D: Seasonal weather changes causing the model's accuracy to drift

questions.key_concept: Model extraction rebuilds a model from its query responses; detailed scores and unlimited queries make it easier.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an attacker could learn by sending many queries and keeping every answer.
questions.correct_explanation: Full-precision scores and unlimited queries let a subscriber send many inputs, record the answers and train a near-equivalent copy of the model, a model extraction attack. The firm loses the asset it sells, and the copy can help plan further attacks. Heavy query volume could degrade service too, but that is visible and can be throttled, while extraction quietly takes the product itself.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because unlimited queries invite overload. But slowdowns are visible and fixed by throttling; the quieter, costlier threat is a copy of the proprietary model.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because poisoning is a major AI threat. But routine queries do not retrain a deployed model unless they feed its training data, which nothing here suggests.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because drift affects every model. But drift comes from changing conditions, not from how the API is exposed, so it is not a threat this design creates.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes queries retrain a deployed model, which they do not unless fed into training, and D is drift from changing conditions, not a threat the API creates.
Final two: B beats A because rebuilding the model quietly takes the asset being sold; overload is visible and can be throttled.
Exam cue: detailed confidence scores plus unlimited queries point to model extraction; look for query limits and coarser outputs.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.4.4 (Model Extraction); MITRE ATLAS AML.T0024.002 (Extract AI Model)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.1 Attacks on Data and Models (extraction through an inference API). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA pilot, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: An energy supplier's AI model that schedules disconnections for unpaid bills has flagged five times more households in one region since Monday. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Retrain the model on last month's data to restore normal rates
options.B: Log the spike for the next quarterly model performance review
options.C: Pause the disconnections and preserve the model's inputs and outputs
options.D: Find the root cause before changing anything in how the model operates

questions.key_concept: AI incident containment disengages the harmful action and preserves inputs, outputs and versions for root cause analysis.
questions.pre_read: Ask who is being harmed right now and what would stop it without destroying evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: Disconnection harms households directly, so the first step is to stop the harm: pause the automated action through the mechanism for disengaging the model, and keep its inputs, outputs and version for investigation. Root cause analysis must follow, but diagnosing first means households keep losing power while analysts work, and the evidence it needs is safest when preserved at the start.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retraining can fix data problems. But retraining before the cause is known may repeat the fault, overwrites evidence and is itself an unapproved change.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because routine reviews handle model performance. But a sudden spike that cuts off households is an incident harming people now, not a quarterly metric.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because root cause matters. But diagnosis takes time and households keep losing service meanwhile; containment comes first, with evidence preserved so the cause can still be found.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains before the cause is known and overwrites evidence, and B pushes an incident that is harming households now into a routine review.
Final two: C beats D because containment stops the harm while preserved records still allow root cause analysis; diagnosing first lets the harm continue.
Exam cue: in an AI incident harming people, disengage the model or its action first and preserve inputs, outputs and versions; root cause comes next.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2G.2 Containment: Disengage, Roll Back and Preserve Evidence (stop the harm and keep the evidence, then fix). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA pilot, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A help desk rolled back its ticket-routing model, which learns from agents' corrections, and closed the incident; one contractor account had submitted thousands of corrections. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain at once on the recent corrections to restore accuracy
options.B: Treat the event as normal drift and tighten monitoring
options.C: Disable the contractor account and keep the rolled-back model in place
options.D: Reopen the incident and probe suspected poisoning before retraining

questions.key_concept: A suspected poisoning incident stays open until the poisoned data and the gap that let it in are removed; rollback only contains it.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the cause is still present somewhere the model will learn from again.
questions.correct_explanation: Closing the incident after a rollback treats the symptom of what looks like deliberate manipulation, a security incident whose cause is still in place. Thousands of corrections from one account suggest data poisoning, and those records may still sit in the training data, ready to return at the next retraining. Reopening it finds them and the gap that let them in. Disabling the account removes one source but leaves the bad data and weak controls.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retraining refreshes the model. But training on all recent corrections would feed the suspect data straight back in and destroy evidence of what happened.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because routing quality changed over time. But drift comes from natural change; thousands of corrections from one account point to deliberate manipulation.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it stops the suspect source. But the poisoned corrections may remain in the training data, and nothing fixes the feedback controls that let one account submit so many.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains on the suspect corrections, reintroducing the fault, and B labels deliberate manipulation as drift, which comes from natural change.
Final two: D beats C because root cause analysis finds the poisoned data and the control gap; disabling one account leaves both in place.
Exam cue: when an AI incident may be deliberate manipulation, rollback contains it but does not end it; remove the poisoned data and the gap that let it in before retraining.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 RS.AN-03 (Root cause of the incident established); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.3 (Poisoning Attacks and Mitigations)

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Retrieval content
questions.question: A Finnish building-materials maker's HR assistant answers staff questions using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over files, including manager-only salary reviews, through one service account. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the data owner limit retrieval to files each user may open
options.B: Add an output filter that masks salary figures in answers
options.C: Limit the assistant's service account to read access on those files
options.D: Remind staff in training not to ask about colleagues' pay

questions.key_concept: Content used for retrieval-augmented generation needs a data owner and access rights that follow the asking user, not the assistant's service account.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose permissions the assistant uses when it fetches a file, and who can then read the answer.
questions.correct_explanation: Retrieval runs under the assistant's single service account, so any employee who asks can receive content from files they could never open, salary reviews included. The data owner must decide what may be indexed, and retrieval must enforce each user's own access rights. An output filter that masks salary figures helps, but it misses anything else in those files, and rephrased requests can bypass it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it blocks the most obvious leak. But it masks salary figures only, not the rest of each file, and rephrased requests can bypass a filter.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because least privilege suits service accounts. But read access still lets the assistant read salary reviews and repeat them to anyone who asks.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because awareness reduces misuse. But an innocent question can still pull salary content into an answer, and training cannot change what the assistant can reach.

tips: Eliminate: C limits the account to read access, though reading is how restricted content reaches answers, and D relies on staff training, which cannot limit what the assistant retrieves.
Final two: A beats B because access rights at retrieval keep restricted content out of every answer; a salary filter catches one field, and rephrased requests can bypass it.
Exam cue: for RAG, check that retrieval respects each user's rights and that the data owner approved what is indexed; output filters are a backstop, not the control.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy)

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Label files
questions.question: A Kazakh railway's contractor sends corrected label files for its track-defect model under the same file names, replacing the earlier files before each retraining. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the data team recheck a sample of the corrected labels
options.B: Add more labeled images so single label errors matter less
options.C: Require a contract warranty that every delivered label is accurate
options.D: Version each label delivery and link it to the model it trained

questions.key_concept: Labels are training data: lineage must tie each model version to the exact label set it learned from.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether anyone could say, after a fault, exactly which data the live model learned from.
questions.correct_explanation: Labels are part of the training data, so overwriting them breaks lineage: after a missed defect, nobody could show which labels trained the live model, reproduce it or trace the fault to its data. Versioning each delivery and linking it to the model it trained restores that trail. Rechecking a sample of corrected labels is useful quality work, but it says nothing about which labels a deployed model learned from.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because label quality matters. But a quality check on today's files cannot show which labels earlier model versions learned from once those files are overwritten.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because volume can smooth random noise. But more images do not restore the lost record of which labels trained each model, and systematic label errors persist.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because contracts shift some liability. But a warranty is a vendor claim; it gives no lineage and cannot show which labels a model used.

tips: Eliminate: B adds volume, which neither restores lineage nor fixes systematic label errors, and C leans on a warranty, which is a vendor claim, not a record.
Final two: D beats A because versioned label sets tie each model to the data it learned from; a quality recheck improves today's labels but leaves that trail broken.
Exam cue: labels are training data; expect each model version to trace to an exact, kept version of its data and labels.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SR-4 (Provenance); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-07 (Inventories of data and metadata maintained)

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Scholarship data
questions.question: A Nigerian scholarship fund will train a model on ten years of officers' award decisions, in which rural applicants with similar grades won far less often. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the model owner add more rural records to the training data
options.B: Remove applicants' home location from the model's inputs
options.C: Have the model owner assess past decisions for bias before training
options.D: Test the trained model's accuracy on a holdout of recent decisions

questions.key_concept: Past human decisions used as labels carry their bias into a model; accuracy measured against them rewards repeating it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the model is being taught to copy, and whether copying it well is what the fund wants.
questions.correct_explanation: The labels are officers' past awards, which disadvantaged rural applicants with similar grades, so a model trained on them learns to repeat that pattern. The owner must assess the labels for historical bias and decide how to correct it before training. Holdout testing sounds rigorous, but a holdout drawn from the same decisions scores the model on how faithfully it copies them, so high accuracy would hide the bias.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more data often helps. But more past decisions carry the same skew, so the model learns the same disadvantage with more confidence.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it removes the obvious input. But other inputs, such as school or district, can stand in for location and carry the same bias.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because holdout testing is sound practice. But a holdout from the same biased decisions rewards the model for copying them, so high accuracy would hide the problem.

tips: Eliminate: A adds more of the same skewed decisions, and B drops one input, though proxies such as school or district can carry the same bias.
Final two: C beats D because the labels themselves are biased; accuracy against biased labels measures how well the model copies the bias.
Exam cue: when labels are past human decisions, ask whether those decisions were fair before training; accuracy against them proves agreement, not fairness.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.7 (Fair with Harmful Bias Managed)

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Customer ratings
questions.question: A Colombian food-delivery app retrains its restaurant-ranking model on customer star ratings, which come from 4% of orders, mostly after couriers arrive late. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The model may learn delivery delays, not restaurant quality
options.B: Restaurants may post fake ratings to push up their own rankings
options.C: Ratings from 4% of orders are too few records to train on
options.D: The model may not be retrained often enough to track tastes

questions.key_concept: Labels must measure what the model is meant to predict; skewed or off-target labels teach the wrong lesson however many there are.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the label really measures and who supplies it, before asking how much of it there is.
questions.correct_explanation: Ratings come mostly after couriers arrive late, so they largely measure delivery delays, and they come from a small slice of customers. A model retrained on them can learn to demote restaurants for delays they may not have caused. Fake ratings are a real poisoning risk for any rating-fed model, but nothing here points to manipulation; the stated problem is that honest labels measure the wrong thing.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because rating systems invite manipulation. But the stem points to who rates and when, not to fake reviews; honest ratings here still measure the wrong thing.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because small samples are weak. But the stated flaw is who rates and when; more ratings of the same kind would still mostly reflect late deliveries.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because customer tastes change. But retraining more often on the same skewed ratings would relearn delivery delays, not restaurant quality.

tips: Eliminate: C treats the issue as volume, though more ratings of the same kind would reflect the same delays, and D retrains more often, which relearns the same skewed labels.
Final two: A beats B because the stated fact is what the labels measure; fake ratings are a real risk, but nothing here suggests them.
Exam cue: check what a label actually measures and who supplies it; skewed or off-target labels teach the wrong lesson at any volume.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Tuning rounds
questions.question: A Saudi desalination plant's data scientists tuned a membrane-fouling model over 40 rounds, checking each round's score on the test set, then reported that score. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Each tuning round went ahead without the model owner's approval
options.B: The rounds may have overfitted the model to its training data
options.C: The reported score is no longer an unseen test of performance
options.D: The score was not compared with a simpler baseline model

questions.key_concept: A test set used to guide tuning stops being an unseen check; its score overstates performance on new data.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the test data influenced any design choice before the final score was taken.
questions.correct_explanation: Each round's settings were chosen by looking at test-set scores, so over 40 rounds the model was fitted to that test set. Its final score is no longer an unseen check and will likely overstate performance on new plant data. Overfitting to training data is a related worry, but the stated fact is worse: the set meant to stay untouched was used to tune, so no unseen check remains.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because approvals matter. But tuning rounds are development work; the owner's approval belongs at the release gate, not on each experiment.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because heavy tuning can overfit. But the stated flaw is the test set guiding tuning, which inflates the reported score whatever the training fit.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because baselines show whether tuning paid off. But the tuned model's score on the reused test set is inflated, so any comparison would flatter it.

tips: Eliminate: A asks for approval of each experiment, though the gate is at release, and D adds a baseline comparison, which the inflated score would still distort.
Final two: C beats B because the test set itself guided 40 rounds of choices, so its score is no longer an unseen check of performance.
Exam cue: once test data shapes design or tuning choices, it is no longer a test set; expect a fresh holdout for the final score.

questions.question: A Norwegian salmon farm's sea-lice model, validated for monthly lice-trend reports to managers, now also decides when individual pens get chemical treatment. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Treat the existing validation as covering the treatment decisions too
options.B: Retrain the model on past treatment records before wider use
options.C: Take the new use back through the design and validation gates
options.D: Monitor treatment outcomes closely during the first season

questions.key_concept: Validation holds only for the purpose it was done for; a new use goes back through the lifecycle's design and validation gates.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the model was validated to do with what it is now being used to decide.
questions.correct_explanation: Validation showed the model's counts were good enough for monthly trend reports; it never showed they are accurate enough, pen by pen, to decide chemical treatment, which carries new impacts on fish welfare, cost and the environment. A new purpose needs its own design stage, with intended use and success criteria, then validation against them. Close monitoring in the first season is useful, but it finds problems only after treatments have already been decided.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because nothing in the model changed. But validation covers a stated purpose; the same model making a new decision needs evidence for that decision.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because treatment data seems relevant. But retraining is a technical fix made before the new use's purpose and success criteria are even defined.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because close watching catches problems. But it is detective: treatments are decided first, and nobody has defined what a good treatment decision looks like.

tips: Eliminate: A carries validation over to a purpose it never covered, and B retrains before the new use's purpose and criteria are defined.
Final two: C beats D because the gates set criteria and evidence before treatment decisions rely on the model; monitoring finds problems only afterward.
Exam cue: when a model is put to a new use, expect it to re-enter the lifecycle at design; earlier validation covers only the old purpose.

questions.question: An Indonesian e-wallet routes 20% of live loan applications to an unvalidated challenger model whose decisions take effect, to compare it with the current model. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Treat the live comparison as the challenger's agile validation
options.B: Reduce the challenger's share of live applications to 5%
options.C: Let the challenger score applications in shadow mode until validated
options.D: Rely on the challenger's strong results in offline development tests

questions.key_concept: A live test whose decisions take effect is a deployment; unvalidated models can be compared in shadow mode, scoring cases without deciding them.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the model under test is changing real outcomes for real people yet.
questions.correct_explanation: When the challenger's decisions take effect, one in five applicants is decided by a model that has not passed validation, so the comparison is really an ungated release. In shadow mode, the challenger scores the same live applications but its outputs are not used, giving deployment-like evidence without harm. Cutting its share to 5% shrinks the exposure, but those applicants are still decided by an unvalidated model.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because agile delivery favors fast feedback from production. But a test whose decisions take effect is a release, and the model must pass its gate before deciding real loans.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a smaller share means fewer people affected. But every applicant in that share is still decided by a model that has not passed validation.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the results look strong. But development tests are the builders' own and have not passed the release gate; live conditions may differ.

tips: Eliminate: A counts live agile testing as validation, though its decisions already take effect, and D relies on the builders' own development tests, which are not the release gate.
Final two: C beats B because shadow scoring gathers live evidence while nobody is decided by the unvalidated model; a smaller share still exposes real applicants.
Exam cue: if a model's outputs take effect, it is deployed; compare unvalidated models in shadow mode, scoring live cases without deciding them.

questions.question: A Bangladeshi jute mill plans to log operators' spoken safety reports with an open-source speech model whose model card says it was never tested on Bengali. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Fine-tune the model on the mill's own Bengali safety reports first
options.B: Have the model owner test it on Bengali safety reports before use
options.C: Rely on the model's high published accuracy in other languages
options.D: Have the model owner review the open-source code before use

questions.key_concept: A model card's stated limits mark where evidence is missing; using a model beyond them needs the organization's own testing first.
questions.pre_read: Read the model's documented limits, then compare them with the planned use.
questions.correct_explanation: The model card itself warns that performance on Bengali is unknown, and mistranscribed safety reports could hide hazards. The model owner must first test the model on real Bengali safety reports against agreed criteria. Fine-tuning on the mill's own reports may help later, but it inherits the base model's unknowns and still needs the same testing, so choosing it first commits to a fix before any evidence.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tuning adapts a model to local data. But it inherits the base model's unknowns and still needs testing; committing to it first skips the evidence.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because published scores look strong. But they describe other languages and data; the model card itself says Bengali was never tested.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because open code seems transparent. But reading code cannot show how a trained model behaves on Bengali speech; only testing on that use can.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on scores from other languages, which say nothing about Bengali, and D treats readable code as evidence of behavior, which only testing gives.
Final two: B beats A because testing the intended use comes before investing in a fix; tuning inherits the base model's unknowns and still needs testing.
Exam cue: when a model card lists a limit that matches the planned use, expect testing on that use before any reliance or tuning.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Retiring a tuned model
questions.question: A Maltese dating app is retiring a vendor-hosted translation model it fine-tuned on members' messages; logs are archived and staff access revoked, but the vendor was never contacted. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The vendor may still hold the tuned model and members' messages
options.B: Archived logs may hold more members' messages than are needed
options.C: The vendor may keep billing for the model until the contract ends
options.D: The IS auditor did not approve the model's retirement plan

questions.key_concept: Retiring a vendor-hosted model includes the vendor's copies: the tuned model and its training data need a recorded keep-or-delete decision.
questions.pre_read: List every place the model and its training data live, including outside the organization.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning at a vendor leaves a model shaped by members' messages, and often the messages themselves, on the vendor's systems. Revoking staff access ends use but not that copy, which stays outside the company's control with no keep-or-delete decision. Over-retained archived logs are a real minimization issue, but archived logs stay under the company's own control, where any excess can be found and removed.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because data minimization is a real duty. But archived logs stay under the company's control; the vendor's copies do not, and nobody has asked about them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because exit costs matter. But billing is a commercial matter; the retirement gap is members' messages and a tuned model left outside the company's control.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because audit often reviews retirement plans. But the model owner approves retirement; the IS auditor assesses the plan and never approves it.

tips: Eliminate: C raises billing, a commercial matter rather than a retirement control, and D gives the IS auditor an approval role the model owner holds.
Final two: A beats B because the vendor's copies sit outside the company's control; archived logs remain where the company can still correct them.
Exam cue: for vendor-hosted or tuned models, retirement must reach the vendor's copies of the model and its training data, not just internal access.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.7 (Decommissioning AI systems safely); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-9 (External System Services)

questions.question: A Slovak bottled-water producer swapped the weather feed its demand model uses for a cheaper provider, logging it only as a supplier change. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Close the supplier change once the model's code is confirmed unchanged
options.B: Retrain the demand model now on the new feed's past data
options.C: Have procurement review the new supplier's data quality record
options.D: Treat the feed swap as an AI change with impact testing

questions.key_concept: Changing a model's input data source changes its behavior, so it needs change control and testing even when no code changes.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the edit changes what the model sees, not just whether it changes code.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's forecasts depend on its inputs, so a new weather provider, with different coverage, timing or measurement, can shift every demand forecast while the code and version stay identical. The swap needs an impact assessment, testing of forecasts against acceptance criteria and the model owner's approval, like any change. Procurement's review of the supplier is useful due diligence, but it cannot show how this model's forecasts change.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because change control often tracks code and versions. But a model's behavior also depends on its inputs, and a new feed can shift every forecast.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it aligns the model with the new feed. But retraining is itself a change, made before anyone has measured the swap's effect.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because supplier due diligence matters. But a supplier's quality record cannot show how this model's forecasts change on the new feed.

tips: Eliminate: A treats unchanged code as no change, though inputs drive model behavior, and B retrains, itself a change, before the swap's effect is measured.
Final two: D beats C because only testing the model on the new feed shows the effect on forecasts; supplier checks describe the data, not the model's behavior.
Exam cue: a new data source, feature or feed is an AI change; expect impact testing and model owner approval even when no code changes.

questions.question: A Taiwanese chip fab rolled its wafer-defect model back to the prior version after a bad release, but the new release's alert threshold stayed live. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have an engineer reset the alert threshold to the prior value now
options.B: Version each model with its threshold and settings for rollback
options.C: Retrain the restored model so it suits the new threshold
options.D: Confirm the restored model matches the prior approved version

questions.key_concept: A rollback must restore a known good state: the model version together with the thresholds and settings approved with it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what besides the model file decides the system's outputs, and whether rollback restores it too.
questions.correct_explanation: The model's alerts depend on both the model and its threshold, so restoring one without the other produced a combination nobody approved or tested. A baseline that versions each model with its threshold and settings lets rollback return a known good state every time. Resetting the threshold by hand fixes this occurrence, but it is a manual change outside change control, and the next rollback would repeat the gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it restores the prior pairing quickly. But a manual reset bypasses change control, and the next rollback would leave the same gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it makes the pair consistent. But it fits a sound model to a setting nobody approved for it, and retraining is itself a change.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a rollback should restore the approved version. But the model file is not the gap; it now runs with a threshold nobody tested it with.

tips: Eliminate: C fits a sound model to a setting nobody approved for it, and D checks the model file, though the untested part is the threshold left behind.
Final two: B beats A because a baseline that versions settings with the model fixes every future rollback; a manual reset fixes only this one, outside change control.
Exam cue: an AI configuration baseline covers the model version plus its thresholds, prompts and settings; rollback restores them together.

questions.question: An Italian eyewear maker's lens-defect model began misgrading after routine server patching updated its image-processing library; the model and its code were unchanged. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Exempt the inspection servers from routine patching
options.B: Leave library updates to the server team's patch process
options.C: Baseline the model's libraries and regression-test it after patches
options.D: Compare monthly defect grades with a manual inspection of sampled lenses

questions.key_concept: A model's behavior depends on the libraries that prepare its inputs, so they belong in its baseline and their updates need model regression tests.
questions.pre_read: Ask what else, beyond the model file and code, shapes what the model sees and outputs.
questions.correct_explanation: The image-processing library prepares the images the model sees, so updating it changed the model's behavior without touching the model or its code. Listing such libraries in the model's configuration baseline, and rerunning a fixed set of graded images after patches, catches this before lenses are misgraded. A monthly comparison with manual inspection would detect the problem, but only after weeks of wrong grades.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it stops the trigger. But unpatched servers carry security risk; the fix is controlling how patches reach the model, not avoiding them.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the patch process already exists. But it tests that servers work, not that the model still grades lenses correctly after a library changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because comparing with manual grades is strong evidence. But monthly checks find the problem weeks after misgrading starts; testing before release prevents it.

tips: Eliminate: A trades a model risk for a security risk by skipping patches, and B relies on server patch tests, which do not check the model's grades.
Final two: C beats D because regression tests after each patch stop misgrading before it starts; monthly comparisons find it weeks later.
Exam cue: an AI baseline includes the libraries a model depends on; library and platform updates need model regression tests, not just server checks.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Base model retirement
questions.question: A Tunisian call-center outsourcer will redo the fine-tuning of the model that scores its staff's calls, because the vendor is replacing the base model with a successor. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Reuse the earlier validation for the unchanged tuning data and settings
options.B: Have the vendor certify the successor's accuracy for call scoring
options.C: Switch over, then compare scores with the old model for a month
options.D: Validate the re-tuned model as a new model before it scores calls

questions.key_concept: The same tuning on a different base model produces a different model; it needs fresh validation before it replaces the old one.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether anything that shapes the model's behavior has changed, even if your own inputs have not.
questions.correct_explanation: A fine-tuned model's behavior comes from its base model as well as the tuning data, so repeating the same tuning on a successor base produces a new model with possibly different scores for the same calls. It needs validation against the acceptance criteria before it scores staff calls. Running it live and comparing scores for a month would show differences, but only after staff have been scored by an unvalidated model.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the outsourcer's own inputs are unchanged. But the base model changed, and tuning on a different base yields a different model with untested behavior.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor knows its model. But a vendor certificate is an input, and it cannot cover how the outsourcer's own tuning behaves on the new base.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because comparing with the old model is useful evidence. But switching first means staff are scored by an unvalidated model for a month.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes unchanged tuning means an unchanged model, though the base changed, and B relies on a vendor certificate, which is an input, not validation.
Final two: D beats C because validation must come before the new model scores staff; switching first and comparing later lets an untested model decide.
Exam cue: a vendor's base-model change makes your tuned model a new model; expect revalidation before it is used, whatever stayed the same on your side.

questions.question: A humanitarian agency in Jordan lets a model stop families' food vouchers automatically when it flags them as duplicate registrations; a supervisor reviews weekly totals. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have a caseworker approve each stop before it takes effect
options.B: Have the supervisor review a sample of stops each week
options.C: Rely on the model's validation results to justify automatic stops
options.D: Restrict automatic stops to flags with very high model confidence

questions.key_concept: The oversight model must match impact: decisions that cut essentials like food need a person to approve each one before it takes effect.
questions.pre_read: Ask how much harm one wrong automated decision does, and when a person first sees it.
questions.correct_explanation: Stopping a family's food vouchers causes serious, immediate harm, so a wrong flag must be caught before it takes effect. Human-in-the-loop review, a caseworker approving each stop, matches oversight to that impact. A weekly sample review by the supervisor adds some human checking, but it comes after the fact: most wrong stops go unseen, and those found have already cut families' food.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it adds human review. But sampling after the fact leaves most wrong stops unseen, and any it finds have already cut a family's food.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because validation shows the model works on average. But a strong validation result does not stop individual wrong flags from cutting essential support.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because confident flags are wrong less often. But confidence is the model's own estimate; a confident wrong flag still cuts a family's food with nobody checking first.

tips: Eliminate: C treats validation results as a reason to remove human checks, and D trusts the model's own confidence, which can be high on a wrong flag.
Final two: A beats B because approval before each stop prevents harm; a weekly sample finds a few wrong stops after families have lost food.
Exam cue: match the oversight model to impact; when one wrong decision cuts essentials, expect a human in the loop, not just after-the-fact sampling.
