questions.question: A Mongolian herder-insurance provider's assessors override 18% of a model's livestock-loss payout recommendations, each with a reason code that nobody reviews. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Require a manager to approve each override reason before any payout
options.B: Have the model owner analyze override reasons for error patterns
options.C: Remove the override option so payouts stay consistent
options.D: Have the model owner retrain the model on the overridden cases now

questions.key_concept: Overrides are evidence about the model; analyze their reasons, and avoid making disagreement harder than agreement.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the assessors' disagreements could tell the owner about the model.
questions.correct_explanation: An 18% override rate means the model and the assessors often disagree, and the reason codes record why. Analyzing them shows whether errors cluster by region, herd type or season, and feeds monitoring and fixes through change control. Manager approval of each override sounds like tighter control, but it makes disagreeing harder than agreeing, which breeds automation bias, and still leaves the reasons unread.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because approval looks like stronger control. But extra friction on disagreeing pushes assessors to accept the model, and approving reasons one by one never analyzes them for patterns.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because consistency sounds fair. But removing overrides removes human oversight, leaving every model error to reach herders unchecked.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because overridden cases look like ready labels. But some overrides may be wrong too; retraining before analysis is a change made without knowing the cause.

tips: Eliminate: C removes human oversight to gain consistency, and D retrains on overrides before anyone knows whether the model or the assessors were right.
Final two: B beats A because analyzing reasons finds the model's error patterns; approval for each override adds friction that pushes assessors toward agreeing.
Exam cue: overrides are monitoring data; expect their reasons to be analyzed, and be wary of controls that make disagreeing with the model harder.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.1 (Post-deployment monitoring including appeal, override, incident response and change management); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed)

questions.question: A Pakistani mobile-banking app's input drift metrics stay within tolerance, yet confirmed fraud its model missed has tripled since scammers changed tactics. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Tighten the input drift thresholds so alerts fire sooner
options.B: Lower the fraud alert threshold so the model flags more payments
options.C: Monitor detection rates against confirmed fraud outcomes
options.D: Keep uptime and response time as the fraud model's main indicators

questions.key_concept: Concept drift changes the link between inputs and outcomes, which input metrics can miss; monitoring against real outcomes, such as confirmed missed fraud, reveals it.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the indicator in place could change at all if the meaning of the inputs changed.
questions.correct_explanation: Scammers changed tactics, so the link between inputs and fraud shifted while the inputs themselves look much the same: concept drift. Input drift metrics cannot see that, which is why they stay green while missed fraud triples. Tracking detection against confirmed fraud outcomes, with thresholds that trigger review, shows decay directly. Tighter input thresholds only make the same blind measure more sensitive; they would still miss a change in meaning.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because sensitive alerts catch drift sooner. But the inputs have not shifted much; the change is in what they mean, which input metrics cannot measure.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because flagging more seems to catch more fraud. But it is a change made without measuring decay, and new tactics may never score high enough.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because availability is easy to measure. But a model can run perfectly while missing fraud; uptime says nothing about decision quality.

tips: Eliminate: B lowers the threshold, a change made without any measure of decay, and D tracks availability, which says nothing about decision quality.
Final two: C beats A because concept drift shows only in outcomes; tighter input thresholds sharpen a measure that cannot see changes in meaning.
Exam cue: inputs steady but results worse points to concept drift; recommend monitoring against real outcomes, not just input distributions.

questions.question: A French city's AI traffic-signal model is measured only on its travel-time target, which it meets, but residents report pedestrian waits near a care home have doubled. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the approved travel-time target as the model's main measure
options.B: Have the model owner assess and monitor impacts on pedestrians
options.C: Retrain the model now so that pedestrian waiting times weigh more heavily
options.D: Recheck travel-time accuracy on a fresh sample of junctions

questions.key_concept: Monitoring covers a system's impacts on people, not just its target metric; owners set impact indicators and thresholds within approved tolerances before tuning.
questions.pre_read: Ask who bears the cost of what the model optimizes, and whether anyone measures it.
questions.correct_explanation: The model optimizes travel time, and its effect on people crossing near the care home is not measured. The model owner needs to assess that effect and monitor impact indicators, such as pedestrian waits at sensitive crossings, with thresholds inside approved tolerances. Retraining to weigh pedestrian waits may be the owner's eventual fix, but it is a design choice, and without those indicators nobody can show it worked or spot the next side effect.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model meets its approved target. But a target on travel time says nothing about harm to pedestrians, which nobody measures.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it addresses the complaint directly. But without impact indicators nobody can show the fix worked or spot new side effects, and retraining is a change.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fresh data checks accuracy. But the model's travel-time accuracy is not in doubt; its effects on pedestrians are what go unmeasured.

tips: Eliminate: A treats meeting the target as enough, though targets omit side effects, and D rechecks travel-time accuracy, which is not in question.
Final two: B beats C because the harm must be measured before a retrain can be judged; tuning first fixes one symptom without a measure.
Exam cue: supervise impacts on people, not just the metric a model optimizes; expect indicators and thresholds for the groups it affects.

questions.question: A Swiss city's school-placement model, retrained each spring, assigns children to schools; families can appeal, but its decision log keeps only each child's final placement. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Log each placement's inputs and model version with the outcome
options.B: Have staff rerun disputed cases through the current model version
options.C: Publish how the placement model weighs each input
options.D: Keep the placement log longer so appeals can be answered

questions.key_concept: A decision log must hold each decision's inputs and model version, so a contested outcome can be explained and reviewed.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a reviewer would need to see to explain one family's placement months later.
questions.correct_explanation: An appeal needs what the model was given and which version decided; a log of outcomes alone can explain neither. Logging inputs and model version with each placement makes every decision traceable. Rerunning disputed cases through the current version sounds like reperformance, but without the original inputs staff may not rerun the same case, and a since-retrained model shows today's answer, not why the original placement was made.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because rerunning looks like reperformance. But without the original inputs the case may differ, and a changed model gives today's answer, not the original reason.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because transparency helps families understand. But a general description of weights cannot explain or correct one child's placement.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because longer retention supports appeals. But keeping outcome-only records longer adds nothing about why each placement was made.

tips: Eliminate: C explains the model in general, not one child's placement, and D keeps the same outcome-only records longer, which adds no explanation.
Final two: A beats B because logged inputs and version let reviewers trace the actual decision; rerunning today's model may use different inputs and a different model.
Exam cue: for contestable AI decisions, a log needs inputs, model version, output and final action; outcomes alone cannot support an appeal.

questions.question: A Tanzanian health ministry will launch a generative AI assistant answering pregnancy questions by text message. Which acceptance criterion should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Share of sampled answers that pilot users rate as helpful
options.B: Average response time of under two seconds per text message
options.C: Accuracy on the vendor's standard medical question-answer benchmark
options.D: Cap on unsafe or invented advice in clinician-reviewed tests

questions.key_concept: Acceptance criteria for generative AI include a limit on confabulated or unsafe answers, set before testing and judged by qualified reviewers.
questions.pre_read: Ask who could tell a fluent wrong answer from a right one, and whether the criterion relies on them.
questions.correct_explanation: A pregnancy assistant's worst failures are confident answers that are false, known as confabulation, or advice that is unsafe. Only clinicians reviewing realistic scenarios can catch them, so the key criterion is a cap on such answers, set before testing. Users' helpfulness ratings matter, but users cannot judge medical accuracy, and a confident wrong answer often feels most helpful.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because user acceptance matters. But pilot users cannot tell accurate medical advice from confident invention, so high ratings can coexist with harmful answers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because speed affects usability. But a fast answer can still be wrong; response time measures service, not the safety of the advice.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because benchmarks look objective. But a vendor benchmark uses other questions and settings, not pregnancy questions asked by text in this context.

tips: Eliminate: B measures speed, not whether the advice is safe, and C relies on a vendor benchmark built from other questions and settings.
Final two: D beats A because clinicians can spot confident but wrong advice; users rate how helpful an answer feels, not whether it is medically right.
Exam cue: for generative AI giving advice, expect a pre-set limit on confabulated or unsafe answers, judged by qualified reviewers on realistic scenarios.

questions.question: In validation, a Belgian student-loan fund's model approved the same share of Dutch- and French-speaking applicants, but wrongly declined creditworthy French speakers three times as often. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: Equal approval shares show the model treats both language groups fairly
options.B: One fairness measure is met while error rates show unequal harm
options.C: Removing language from the inputs would make the model fair
options.D: The model has drifted since its training data was collected

questions.key_concept: Fairness measures can conflict: equal approval rates can coexist with unequal error rates, so owners must choose and justify the measures used.
questions.pre_read: Ask which fairness measure the claim rests on, and what a different measure shows.
questions.correct_explanation: Equal approval shares satisfy one fairness measure, but creditworthy French speakers are wrongly declined three times as often, so the harm of errors falls unequally. Fairness measures can conflict; the model owner, with legal input, must choose which apply and justify the choice, and the IS auditor reports this unequal harm. Treating equal approval shares as proof of fairness reads one measure as the whole picture.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because equal outcomes look fair. But equal approval shares can mask unequal errors; here creditworthy French speakers are wrongly declined three times as often.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because dropping the attribute seems neutral. But other inputs, such as home province or university, can act as proxies, and only outcome testing shows remaining bias.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because drift is a common AI risk. But these are validation results, before deployment; nothing here shows change over time.

tips: Eliminate: C drops language from the inputs, though proxies can carry the same bias, and D claims drift from validation results, which show no change over time.
Final two: B beats A because fairness measures can conflict; equal approval shares do not show that errors fall evenly across groups.
Exam cue: when a fairness claim rests on one measure, check error rates by group too; the model owner must justify which measures apply.

questions.question: An Ecuadorian flower exporter's pricing assistant can change list prices through a connected tool; its red team tested only the underlying model, with no tool attached. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add an output filter that blocks harmful replies to staff
options.B: Rerun the same red-team tests after each vendor model update
options.C: Ask the vendor for its red-team report on the base model
options.D: Extend red teaming to the deployed assistant and what it can do

questions.key_concept: Red teaming covers the system as deployed, with its tools and permissions; a model-only test cannot show what a manipulated system could do.
questions.pre_read: List what the deployed system can do, then compare it with what the red team actually exercised.
questions.correct_explanation: The red team tested a model that could not act, so nobody knows what a manipulated or mistaken assistant could do to list prices, which is where the harm lies. Red teaming must cover the system as deployed, with its tools, permissions and data sources. Repeating the model-only tests after each update is sound regression practice, but it keeps the same blind spot and never exercises the price changes.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because filters catch harmful text. But a manipulated assistant can change prices without any harmful reply, so a reply filter misses the real harm.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retesting after updates is good practice. But it repeats the same model-only scope and never tests what the assistant can do to prices.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor tested the base model. But that testing cannot cover this assistant's own tool, permissions or pricing context.

tips: Eliminate: A filters replies, though a manipulated assistant can change prices without a harmful reply, and C relies on vendor tests of the base model, not this setup.
Final two: D beats B because the untested risk is what the deployed assistant can do to prices; repeating model-only tests keeps the same blind spot.
Exam cue: red-team the AI system as deployed, with its tools, data sources and permissions; a model-only test cannot show what the system can actually do.

questions.question: An Icelandic avalanche-warning service validated its risk model on complete sensor records, but storms often freeze or cut sensors. Which test should the IS auditor recommend as MOST important before go-live?

options.A: Revalidation by an independent team on the same sensor records
options.B: Robustness testing on degraded and incomplete sensor readings
options.C: A larger validation run on complete records from more seasons
options.D: A load test of the warning website and text alerts during storms

questions.key_concept: Robustness testing feeds a model the degraded inputs it will meet in use, such as missing or frozen readings, before it is relied on.
questions.pre_read: Compare the conditions in the validation data with the conditions on the day the model matters most.
questions.correct_explanation: Validation used complete records, yet storms, when warnings matter most, bring frozen and missing readings the model never saw. Robustness testing with such inputs shows whether it still warns sensibly or fails safely. Independent revalidation adds credibility, but on the same complete records it shares the blind spot: nobody would learn how the model behaves when sensors fail.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because independence strengthens validation. But validators using the same complete records never see storm conditions, so the blind spot remains.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more data seems more thorough. But more complete records repeat the same conditions and never show behavior when sensors fail.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because storms bring traffic spikes. But a load test checks the website and alerts, not whether the model's warnings hold up when readings go missing.

tips: Eliminate: C adds more complete records, which repeat the same conditions, and D tests website capacity, not the model's behavior on bad inputs.
Final two: B beats A because only degraded inputs show how the model behaves in storms; independent validators on the same records share the blind spot.
Exam cue: when inputs in use will be noisier or patchier than in validation, expect robustness testing on those inputs before go-live.

questions.question: A Portuguese cork producer's engineers downloaded a popular pre-trained vision model from a public hub and plan to run it on plant servers for a sorting pilot. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Rely on the model's popularity on the hub as evidence of safety
options.B: Test the model's accuracy on the plant's own cork images
options.C: Verify the model's source and integrity before relying on it
options.D: Add stricter firewall rules around the plant's servers

questions.key_concept: Downloaded models, like other supply-chain components, are untrusted until their source and integrity are verified; model files can carry hidden behavior or code.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the team knows the file it loaded is the one its publisher released, and what it contains.
questions.correct_explanation: A model file from a public hub is a supply-chain component: it may be tampered with, carry a hidden backdoor or, in some file formats, run code when loaded. Treating it as untrusted until its source and integrity are verified, for example against a publisher's hash, comes first. Testing accuracy on the plant's images shows fitness, but a backdoored model can score well while its trigger stays dormant.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because popular models seem well vetted. But downloads are not checks; attackers target popular models, and popularity says nothing about this file's integrity.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because fitness testing is needed anyway. But a tampered model can score well on normal images while carrying a trigger or malicious code.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because firewalls protect servers. But the model came in through an allowed download and runs inside the network; a firewall cannot inspect it.

tips: Eliminate: A takes popularity as proof of safety, which no download count gives, and D adds perimeter rules, though the file arrived through an allowed path.
Final two: C beats B because integrity must be established before relying on any test result; a backdoored model can pass accuracy tests.
Exam cue: treat downloaded models, datasets and libraries as untrusted supply-chain components until their source and integrity are verified.

questions.question: A Lithuanian fertility clinic plans to publish its trained treatment-outcome model, built from patient records, so researchers can download and use it freely. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Researchers rebuilding a working copy of the model from its outputs
options.B: Attackers learning whether a patient's records were used in training
options.C: Researchers using the model on patient records beyond its intended use
options.D: Attackers poisoning the clinic's model by retraining their own copies

questions.key_concept: A released model can leak its training data: membership inference reveals who was in it, which for sensitive data is itself a disclosure.
questions.pre_read: Ask what someone holding the model could learn about the people whose records trained it.
questions.correct_explanation: Once released, the model can be queried without limit, and membership inference can reveal whether a person's records helped train it. Being in a fertility clinic's training data discloses treatment, a serious, irreversible privacy harm. Misuse beyond the intended use is a real concern too, but usage terms and a model card can narrow it, while leaked membership cannot be undone once the model is out.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because extraction is a real AI threat. But the clinic is publishing the model itself; there is nothing left to steal by copying it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because released models get misused. But usage terms and a model card can narrow misuse, while leaked patient membership cannot be taken back.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because poisoning is a major AI threat. But retraining a downloaded copy changes only that copy, not the clinic's own model.

tips: Eliminate: A worries about copying a model that is being published anyway, and D assumes changing a downloaded copy alters the clinic's own model.
Final two: B beats C because revealing who was in a fertility dataset discloses treatment and cannot be undone; misuse can be narrowed by terms and documentation.
Exam cue: before releasing a model trained on sensitive personal data, weigh membership inference and data reconstruction; the model itself can leak who was in it.

questions.question: A Hungarian bike-sharing firm's support chatbot has its rental-database password written into its system prompt; staff say riders cannot see the prompt. Which risk should the IS auditor consider GREATEST?

options.A: Attackers breaching the chatbot's firewall to read the stored prompt
options.B: The vendor logging prompt text, including the password
options.C: Riders losing rental lookups after the password is changed
options.D: Riders prompting the chatbot into revealing the password

questions.key_concept: System prompts can be extracted by prompting, so they are not a safe place for secrets; anything in them may reach any user.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether 'cannot see' means 'cannot obtain' when users can talk to the system.
questions.correct_explanation: Any rider can chat with the bot, and system prompts can often be extracted by asking cleverly, a known direct prompting attack. A password in the prompt is therefore exposed to every anonymous user, who could turn it against the rental database. Vendor logging of prompts would be an exposure too, but to one known party, not to every anonymous rider.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because breaches expose stored data. But extraction needs no breach; riders reach the prompt's contents through the normal chat window.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendors may keep prompt logs. But that exposes the password to one known party; extraction exposes it to every anonymous rider.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rotating credentials can break integrations. But lost lookups are an operational nuisance, not the exposure of a database password to the public.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a firewall breach, though extraction works through the normal chat, and C is an operational nuisance, not an exposure.
Final two: D beats B because extraction opens the password to every anonymous rider; vendor logs expose it to one known party.
Exam cue: treat system prompts as readable by users; secrets in a prompt are exposed, whatever staff believe users can see.

questions.question: A Scottish distillery's AI procurement agent reads emailed invoices and pays each one once its chat log shows a manager's approval. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add a prompt rule requiring approval before each payment
options.B: Cap each agent payment at a small amount to limit losses
options.C: Have finance review the agent's recorded approvals each month
options.D: Enforce approval in the payment system, outside the agent's control

questions.key_concept: Human approval for high-impact agent actions must be enforced outside the model; an approval the agent records itself can be faked or skipped.
questions.pre_read: Ask who, or what, could produce the record that says a manager approved.
questions.correct_explanation: Approval exists only in the agent's own chat log, and the agent reads untrusted invoices, so injected text can fake an approval. Enforcing approval in the payment system, where a manager must act and the agent cannot, makes the control hold whatever the agent is told. Capping each payment reduces the cost of each error, but a manipulated agent could still pay many invoices with no real approval.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because instructions shape agent behavior. But a prompt rule is enforced by the model itself, and injection or error can talk it past the rule.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a cap limits each loss. But a manipulated agent could still pay many capped invoices, each with an approval it recorded itself.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because review catches problems. But monthly review comes after payment, and it checks records the agent itself wrote, which may be false.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a prompt rule the model enforces on itself, and C reviews, after payment, records the agent itself wrote.
Final two: D beats B because approval enforced outside the agent stops unapproved payments; a cap only limits each one while self-recorded approvals continue.
Exam cue: for high-impact agent actions, look for human approval the model cannot grant or record itself.

questions.question: A Croatian disability-benefits office's model that sets home-care hours has exceeded its error tolerance for three weeks; the data team logged it as a backlog item. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Treat it as an AI incident and triage by impact on people
options.B: Schedule retraining for the next quarterly model release
options.C: Escalate it to the security team as a possible breach
options.D: Have the data team find the root cause before acting

questions.key_concept: Performance beyond tolerance in a decision about people is an AI incident, triaged by impact, not a backlog item or a security matter.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether people are being affected right now, and which process is built to respond to that.
questions.correct_explanation: Errors beyond tolerance in a model that sets care hours for people with disabilities are likely affecting their care now, which makes this an AI incident, not routine maintenance. Raising it as an incident and triaging by impact on people decides how fast to contain it, for example by reviewing affected cases or disengaging the model. Root cause analysis is needed, but leading with it leaves wrong care hours in place meanwhile.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retraining through a release is controlled. But it leaves wrong care hours in place for months and skips triage and containment.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because incidents are often security events. But nothing suggests an attack; AI incidents include harmful outputs and tolerance breaches without any breach.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because root cause matters. But diagnosis comes after the incident is raised and triaged; meanwhile people keep receiving wrong care hours.

tips: Eliminate: B queues the fault for a routine release while people are affected, and C routes it as a security breach, though nothing points to an attack.
Final two: A beats D because raising and triaging the incident sets how fast harm is contained; root cause analysis follows, it does not lead.
Exam cue: a tolerance breach in a model that decides about people is an AI incident; raise it, triage by impact on people, then investigate.

questions.question: A South African emergency dispatch center receives four AI incident reports in one morning. Which should the IS auditor expect incident managers to triage FIRST?

options.A: Priority model's error rate on minority-language calls above tolerance
options.B: Website chatbot jailbroken, its insulting replies shared widely online
options.C: Rota-planning model proposing uneven weekend shifts for night dispatchers
options.D: Transcription dashboard down for an hour, with calls still handled

questions.key_concept: Triage ranks AI incidents by likely harm to people, then the business; a quiet tolerance breach in a live model can outrank a visible attack.
questions.pre_read: For each report, ask who is being harmed now, how badly and how many.
questions.correct_explanation: An error rate above tolerance in the call-priority model means some minority-language emergency calls are ranked too low right now, which can delay help to people in danger; it ranks highest on likelihood and impact. The jailbroken chatbot needs follow-up as a security and AI incident, but its harm is reputational and puts no one in danger; a visible attack is not automatically the top priority.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a public, successful attack feels most urgent. But its harm is reputational, while misranked emergency calls can endanger lives now.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fairness to staff matters. But uneven rotas are an internal planning issue a person can correct, with no immediate harm to callers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because outages are classic incidents. But calls were still handled during the hour, so the impact on callers was small and has ended.

tips: Eliminate: C is an internal planning issue with no immediate harm, and D was a short outage during which calls were still handled.
Final two: A beats B because a tolerance breach in a live emergency model harms callers now; the jailbreak's harm is reputational.
Exam cue: triage AI incidents by likelihood and impact on people; a tolerance breach in a live model can outrank a visible attack.

questions.question: After a Peruvian blood bank switched off its generative AI chatbot for showing donors others' appointment details, the privacy officer wants every chat log deleted at once. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Delete the logs now to limit further exposure of donors' data
options.B: Keep the model version and settings, and delete the chat logs
options.C: Keep the logs under restricted access until the investigation ends
options.D: Have the vendor retrain the chatbot on corrected data straight away

questions.key_concept: Incident chat logs are evidence that a generative rerun cannot replace: keep them under restricted access for the investigation, then dispose on schedule.
questions.pre_read: Ask what investigators and affected people will need from these records before deciding to destroy them.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative answers cannot be reliably reproduced later, so the chat logs are the best record of what the chatbot said and whose details it exposed. Deleting them destroys the evidence for root cause, notification and any regulator's questions; restricted access protects donors meanwhile. Keeping the model version and settings looks thorough, but a rerun may never repeat what donors actually saw.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because deletion feels protective. But the chatbot is already off, and deleting logs destroys the evidence needed to find the cause and confirm who was affected.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because version and settings let the chatbot be rerun. But generative answers vary between runs, so only the logs show what donors actually saw.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor can fix the model. But retraining before the cause is known changes the system under investigation and may not fix the fault.

tips: Eliminate: A destroys evidence the investigation needs, though the chatbot is already off, and D changes the system before anyone knows the cause.
Final two: C beats B because only the logs show what the chatbot actually exposed; version and settings make a rerun possible, not a faithful replay.
Exam cue: generative answers cannot be reliably regenerated, so incident logs are primary evidence; restrict access, investigate, then dispose of them on schedule.

questions.question: A Costa Rican park service's chatbot told hikers a closed trail was open; the problem record names 'model hallucination' as root cause and is closed. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Reopen the problem and find why the chatbot gave that answer
options.B: Add a notice that the chatbot's answers may be inaccurate
options.C: Switch to a larger model that hallucinates less often
options.D: Keep the problem closed and note hallucination as a known limit

questions.key_concept: 'Hallucination' names a symptom, not a cause; problem management traces it to data, retrieval, prompt or integration before closing.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the recorded cause would tell anyone what to change so it does not happen again.
questions.correct_explanation: Hallucination, which NIST calls confabulation, describes what the chatbot did, not why. The cause may be a trail-status source that was never updated, retrieval of an old notice or a prompt gap, and each needs a different fix. The problem stays open until that cause is found and a fix verified. A warning notice is a fair extra safeguard, but hikers would still be sent onto closed trails.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because generative AI can be wrong. But a disclaimer leaves the cause in place, and hikers relying on the chatbot would still be sent onto closed trails.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because larger models can be more accurate. But if the trail data or retrieval is the cause, a new model repeats the error; the cause is unknown.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because confabulation is a known limit. But a known limit is a symptom; problem management still needs the specific cause and a verified fix.

tips: Eliminate: C swaps the model before the cause is known, and D accepts a label for the symptom as if it were a root cause.
Final two: A beats B because finding the cause lets it be fixed; a disclaimer leaves hikers exposed to the same wrong answer.
Exam cue: 'the model hallucinated' is like 'operator error': a symptom; expect root cause in data, retrieval, prompt or integration before a problem closes.
